segments.title: The scenario and the fields before entry
sections: A Journal Is Not A P&L Record
The Pre-Entry Fields: What You Decided

cues.text: You open a month of trades and all you can read is the money. A good week, a bad day, a run of small losses you cannot explain.
You try to remember why you took the trade on the 14th, and the memory you find agrees with how it ended.
Your platform already keeps a P and L record: what you entered, what you exited, and what it came to. It is accurate, and it cannot tell you why.
A journal answers two other questions. Why did you take the trade, and did you do what you said you would?
Those are the two you can act on. Your P and L is an excellent historian and a terrible coach.
The journal form has two halves with a seam between them. Everything above the seam exists before the trade resolves, so you can write it down honestly.
One: identity. The date, the instrument, the direction, and the environment, which is live, sim or replay.
Two: the tiers. Your setup, your location, your trigger, and any confirmation, each by name.
Three: construction. Stop price, target price, and size in contracts.
Four: the fill. The intended price, which is the price the plan said you would be filled at, then the actual fill and the entry time.
Five: the grade, which gets its own segment.
Six: the entry tags, the same words every time.
The test number counts how many times price has come to a zone in the session. The first touch is test one, the next is test two.
The session block is early, mid or late, from times you write once on your PlayBook page, the page you keep for each setup.
Skip anything you would have to invent later. A field filled in from memory is a field that agrees with the result.
The rule: every field above the seam, and the entry tags, are written before the exit.
Getting it wrong is a trade logged at 4:30 p.m. with the location chosen to fit where price went, or an intended price left blank because the fill was close enough.
It reveals the record is being written by the result.
The fix: write the intended price on the plan line before the order is armed. A blank field stays blank. An empty field is a smaller problem than a made-up one.

segments.title: The grade
sections: The Grade Is Assigned Before The Outcome

cues.text: Every trade gets one grade: A plus, A, B or C. It is the entry-plan score, assigned at entry, while the result is still unknown.
It comes from four checks you can answer at that moment.
One: is there a named level, and not mid-range?
Two: did a trigger, the price event that puts you in, fire before you entered?
Three: is the stop behind structure, rather than inside the noise?
Four: does the size match the plan for that stop distance?
Now, the grades. All four checks, with the fill within 2 ticks of your intended price, is an A plus.
All four checks is an A.
Three of four, with no breach of the stop or the size, is a B.
Two or fewer, or any breach of the stop or the size, is a C. And C is no trade.
A C in the journal is a trade you took that the table in Module 14 gave no size.
Notice what the list leaves out: how the trade ended. That is deliberate.
cues.chapter: The result is not a check

cues.text: A losing trade can be an A plus. The plan was sound and the market went the other way. That is normal and expected.

A winning trade can be a C, and that is the more useful signal. You were paid for something you would not want to repeat, and a win like that teaches the wrong lesson more convincingly than a loss ever could.
That is not a lucky trade. That is a bad habit with good timing.
The rule: the grade is written at entry from the four checks and the fill gap, and it is never changed after the exit.
Getting it wrong is a B that becomes an A once the target fills, or a grade left blank until the trade plays out.
It reveals the grade has started measuring the outcome, so the one field meant to separate your process from your luck now reads your luck.

The fix: the grade sits above the seam, labelled as the plan, and is saved with the entry. If you want to change one after the exit, leave it, and write the wish as a tag, wanted-regrade. The weekly review counts them.

segments.title: The mark after the exit
sections: The Execution Mark Comes After The Exit

cues.text: The second half of the form, below the seam, stays blank while the trade is open. You fill it in within the hour after the close, in the end-of-day routine from Module 17.
Every field in it is a fact by then. One: the exit, the time and the price.
Two: the outcome. Your R multiple, the result in units of your risk, plus time in trade and commissions.
Three: MAE and MFE. MAE is the most ticks price went against you. MFE is the most it went for you.
Four: the mark, Pass or Fail.
Five: the exit tags. The reason in plain words, and Too Early or Broke Rule where they apply.
Now, the mark. Pass or Fail, assigned after the exit. Did the exit follow the plan? Pass is one of six exits. One: the target.
Two: the planned scale.
Three: a pre-set invalidation, a condition you wrote down before the trade.
Four: the stop.
Five: session end.
Six: a Tier One flatten at T minus 5, being flat five minutes before the biggest scheduled releases.
Anything else is Fail.
Two tags name a Fail. Too Early is a manual exit for any reason other than the four from Module 17, and its mark is Fail, whatever the trade went on to do.
Broke Rule is the tag for breaking one of the hard rules from Module 02, like widening a stop after entry or trading past the kill switch.
Price after your exit is just gossip. It does not change the mark.
The rule: the post-exit fields and the mark are filled in the same day, and every Fail carries the tag that names it.
Getting it wrong is marks filled in days later from memory, or a manual exit marked Pass because it saved a loss.
It reveals the mark is set by how the trade ended, rather than by which exit you took, so a leak in your exits can never show up.
The fix: one test, read off the exit tag. Is the reason on the Pass list? If not, the mark is Fail and the tag is Too Early. An empty mark is filled in before the pre-market routine starts.

segments.title: The cell that teaches most, and the count kept apart
sections: The Cell That Teaches Most: Good Plan, Bad Finish
Your Trades Are Counted Apart From Any Backtest

cues.text: Put the grade and the mark side by side and you get a board of four cells: high grade or low grade, Pass or Fail.
The most instructive cell is a high grade with a failed mark. Right setup, right level, right size, wrong exit.
That is a discipline problem. The read was fine, you broke it afterward, so the work is downstream, while the trade is open.
The reverse cell is a low grade with a passed mark: a poor plan, executed faithfully. That is a selection problem, upstream, at the level and the trigger.
Treat the two the same and you fix the wrong thing. That is repainting the kitchen because the roof leaks.
The rule: before you change anything about a setup, find which cell its trades fall in.
Getting it wrong is dropping a setup after three losses, when two were A plus entries closed by hand.
It reveals you read the column of results instead of the two columns you wrote.
The fix: no setup is changed until you have written its count in each of the four cells. The biggest cell is the one you work on.
Now, your trades are counted apart from any backtest. A backtest assumes a trader who takes every signal at the stated price. Your journal records the real one.
Blend the two and you hide the gap between them. That gap is the thing you are trying to measure.
The same goes for simulated trades. A simulator can hand you fills a live queue would not.
So sim and replay trades count occurrences: how often you saw a setup and followed your process. They never go into an expectancy figure, the average result per trade.
That is what the environment field is for. Set it first, on every trade. The analysis page reports live trades only, with sim and replay beside them.
The rule: the environment field is set on every trade, and no figure you read mixes live with sim or replay.
Getting it wrong is a month of sim trades and three live ones read as one sample.
It reveals you want a bigger number more than an honest one.
The fix: environment is a required field, chosen first. In the weekly review, live counts come first and sim counts sit on a separate line.

check.q: A low grade with a passed mark means...
options: A good plan with bad luck
check.why: A clean exit does not redeem a poor plan. It is a selection problem, upstream at the level and trigger.

check.q: Where do sim and replay trades count?
options: As occurrences, beside the live count
check.why: They count how often you saw a setup and followed your process, and never go into an expectancy figure.

check.q: You drop a setup after three losses, and two of the three were A plus entries closed by hand. What does that reveal?
options: You read results instead of the two columns you wrote
check.why: The fix is to write the count in each of the four cells before changing anything.

cues.text: Once a week, at a fixed time, away from the screen. The time is set in advance.
A bad week does not bring it forward, and a good week does not skip it. Keep it short enough to keep doing.
Read it in this order, count before rate.
One: grades. The count of A plus, A, B and C, and for each grade below A, which check failed.
Two: marks. Pass and Fail counts, Too Early, and the grade by mark board.
Three: the rule-break ledger. Every Broke Rule tag on its own line. Zero is a line too.
Four: the session. Trades per session, with the block and test tags counted.
Five: the fill. How many landed within 2 ticks of the intended price, and which did not.
Six: the excursions. MAE against your stop distance, and R against MFE.
Seven: the sheets. Each pre-market sheet beside the trades, with its readiness score and finish time.
Ignore the weekly P and L. One week is a small sample, and a green week makes every mistake look like a rounding error.

A cohort is a group of your trades that share a field, like a setup. Under 30 trades, or under 20 sessions, the analysis page shows it dimmed. That is the display floor. Read it as a story, not a pattern.
Clearing the floor is a minimum, not a verdict. And the page caps a cohort at two fields at once, because three-way cuts leave cells too small.
Four questions are worth asking.
Which checks failed most often on your lower grades?
Where did you fail the mark, and was it the same place each time?
Did you take trades with no trigger, or a stop inside noise?
What is the one thing you will do differently next week? Pick one. A review that produces five changes produces none.
The rule: the review runs at its fixed time, reads the seven lines in order with each count before its rate, and ends with one change written down.
Getting it wrong is a review held only after a losing week, or one that opens on the balance and ends with five resolutions.
It reveals the review has become a reaction to the result.
The fix: a repeating calendar entry, and a sheet with the seven lines and one blank, the one change. The P and L is not a line on it. The one change becomes next week’s goal in Module 19.

sections: Worked Case: One Trade In Two Halves, One Week Read

cues.text: A composite week, invented prices, belonging to no one. One trade, in two halves.
Above the seam, saved at 9:56 a.m.: long, live, location pd-vah, the short name for the prior-day value area high. All four checks, no fill gap: an A plus.
Below the seam, after the exit: it ended at the stop, which is on the Pass list. Mark: Pass.
Trade two, the same session. An A plus at entry, then a hand exit with no reason from the four. Mark: Fail. Tag: Too Early.
Then the weekly review: eight live trades across five sessions, and no sim.
Grades: three A plus, three A, two B, no C. Both Bs missed the same check: the trigger.
Marks: six Pass, two Fail, both Too Early. One is trade two: right plan, wrong finish.
The ledger is zero, and seven of eight fills landed within 2 ticks. Every cohort is dimmed: eight trades is under the floor.
The one change: exits only at the target, the planned scale, the stop, or one of the four reasons. The account balance was not invited.
Now, score your own journal. Take your last ten trades and last four weeks. One point for each line true of all of them.
One: every field above the seam filled before the exit.
Two: the grade written at entry and never changed.
Three: test number and session block on every trade at a level.
Four: the fields below the seam filled in the same day.
Five: every trade marked, and every Fail carrying its tag.
Six: environment set on every trade, no figure mixing live with sim.
Seven: the review held at its fixed time in all four weeks, ending with one change.
Seven of seven is a journal that can teach you. If line two failed even once, your grades are reading outcomes: fix that first. Otherwise, fix the line with the most misses.
On your next trade, write the intended price and the grade before you send the order. Two fields. That is the whole assignment.
Where it goes next. The four checks, and the size each grade trades, come from one table in Module 14, trade construction.
The post-exit fields and the mark are filled in during the end-of-day routine, Module 17.
Module 19, Toothbrush Therapy, turns grading every trade, and the review’s one change, into daily habits.
Your live trades are the count Module 22, how to test an edge, reads.

check.q: In the composite week, which check did both B grades miss?
check.why: Both Bs failed the same check: the trigger had not fired before entry.

check.q: If line two of your score failed even once, what do you fix first?
options: The grade: it is reading outcomes
check.why: A grade that changes after the exit is reading outcomes, so fix that before anything else.

check.q: What is the assignment before your next session?
options: Write the intended price and the grade before you send the order
check.why: Two fields before the order: the intended price and the grade.

check.q: In the composite week, what was the one change?
options: Exits only at the target, the planned scale, the stop, or one of the four reasons
check.why: The change was about the exits, because the leak was downstream.

questions.q: Which fields are written before the exit?
options: Every field above the seam, and the entry tags
questions.why: Above the seam is everything that exists before the trade resolves.

questions.q: A trade has a named level, a trigger that fired, a stop behind structure and the right size, but the fill is 4 ticks from your intended price. The grade is...
questions.why: All four checks is an A. An A plus needs the fill within 2 ticks.

options: A manual exit because the trade is taking too long
A hand exit that saved a loss
questions.why: The stop is on the Pass list. The other three are manual exits for no reason on the list.

questions.q: A high grade with a Fail points to...
questions.why: The read was fine and the exit broke it, so the work is in what you do while the trade is open.

options: As occurrences, on a separate line from live
Only in the weekly P and L
questions.why: Sim and replay count occurrences. They never go into an expectancy figure.

questions.q: A cohort of 22 trades from 14 sessions is...
questions.why: Below 30 trades, or below 20 sessions, it is shown dimmed, never hidden.

questions.q: You change a grade after the target fills. What does that reveal?
options: The grade has started measuring the outcome
questions.why: The grade is meant to separate process from luck. Changing it after the exit makes it read luck.

questions.q: How many changes does the weekly review end with?
questions.why: Pick one. A review that produces five changes produces none.
